To study unramified morphisms, we need to understand the sheaf of differentials first. 

## Definition of the sheaf of differentials
For schemes $X$ over $Y$, there is a quasicoherent sheaf, $\Omega_{X/Y}$, on $X$. We call it the **sheaf of differentials**. 

:::{#def-sheaf-of-differentials name="sheaf of differentials"}
The sheaf $\Omega_{X/Y}$ is globally defined as the quotient $\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2$, where the ideal sheaf $\mathscr I$ is the sheaf of ideals defining the diagonal embedding $X\to X\times_Y X$. One can check that $\Omega_{X/Y}$ is indeed a sheaf on $X$. We define a map $d\colon \mathscr O_X\to \Omega_{X/Y}$ by $d(f)=\operatorname{pr}_1^*f-\operatorname{pr}_2^*f$ for $f\in \mathscr O_X$.
:::

:::{#prp-local-characterization-of-sheaf-of-differentials name=""}
Affine locally, if $X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ and $Y=\operatorname{Spec}(B)$, then $\Omega_{X/Y}$ is the sheaf associated to the $A$-module $\Omega_{A/B}$, which is generated by symbols $da$ for $a\in A$ subject to the relations:
1. $d(a+a')=da+da'$ for all $a,a'\in A$,
2. $d(aa')=a\,da'+a'\,da$ for all $a,a'\in A$, and
3. $db=0$ for all $b\in B$.
:::

:::{.proof}
By definition, $\Omega_{X/Y}$ is the sheaf associated to the $A$-module $I/I^2$, where $I$ is the kernel of the morphism $A\otimes_B A\to A$. It is generated by elements of the form $a\otimes 1-1\otimes a$ for $a\in A$. One can check that the map $\Omega_{A/B}\xrightarrow I/ I^2$ given by $da\mapsto a\otimes 1-1\otimes a$ is an isomorphism of $A$-modules.
:::

:::{#rem-universal-property-of-differentials name="the universal property"}
The module $\Omega_{A/B}$ is universal for $B$-derivations from $A$ to an $A$-module $M$. We skip the proof here, but one can find it in any standard textbook on algebraic geometry.
:::

## Basic properties of $\Omega_{X/Y}$
There are two standard exact sequences of sheaves of differentials. The first one is the transitivity sequence: for morphisms $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$, there is an exact sequence
$$
f^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Y}\longrightarrow 0.
$$

The second one is the conormal sequence: for a closed immersion $i:X\hookrightarrow Y$ with ideal sheaf $\mathscr I$, there is an exact sequence
$$
\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\longrightarrow i^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow 0.
$$

::: {.callout-note title="Conormal sheaf"}
We call $\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2$ the conormal sheaf of $X$ in $Y$. It is a vector bundle on $X$ if $i:X\hookrightarrow Y$ is a regular immersion. 
:::

The sheaf of differentials $\Omega_{X/Y}$ is compatible with base change: for a cartesian diagram
$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
X' & \xrightarrow{\mu} & X \\
\downarrow & {\square}\,& \downarrow \\
Y' & \longrightarrow & Y
\end{array}
$$
we have a canonical isomorphism
$$
\Omega_{X'/Y'}\cong \mu^*\Omega_{X/Y}.
$$

All these properties can be done by using @prp-local-characterization-of-sheaf-of-differentials and the corresponding properties of $\Omega_{A/B}$.

:::{.callout-tip title="Hint"}
For the two exact sequences, one can check the right one is indeed the cokernel. For the base change property, one can use the universal property of $\Omega_{A/B}$.
:::

Here is a property for $\Omega_{A/B}$. For a localization $S^{-1}A$ of $A$, we have a canonical isomorphism
$$
\Omega_{S^{-1}A/B}\cong S^{-1}\Omega_{A/B}.
$$
One can check this using the universal properties of the module of differentials and localization, or using the explicit description of $\Omega_{A/B}$ in @prp-local-characterization-of-sheaf-of-differentials.

## Easy calculations of some $\Omega_{A/B}$
### A useful lemma
:::{#lem-derivation-of-polynomial-ring name=""}
Let $B$ be a ring and $A=B[x_1,x_2, \cdots]/(r_1, r_2, \cdots)$ be the ring over $B$. Then $\Omega_{A/B}$ is a free $A$-module generated by $dx_1, dx_2, \cdots$ modulo the relations $dr_1, dr_2, \cdots$.
:::
:::{.proof}
For the convenience of the proof, we assume that $A=B[x_1, x_2, \cdots]$. The general case can be reduced to this case by using the transitivity sequence. Let $M=\oplus_i A\,e_i$ be the free $A$-module generated by $e_1, e_2, \cdots$. We define a map $\phi\colon M\to \Omega_{A/B}$ by sending $e_i$ to $dx_i$ in $\Omega_{A/B}$. One can check that $\phi$ is surjective. To show that $\phi$ is injective, we construct an inverse map $\psi\colon \Omega_{A/B}\to M$. For any $a\in A$, we can write it as a polynomial in $x_1, x_2, \cdots,x_n$. We define $\psi(da)$ to be the formal differential of this polynomial. One can check that $\psi$ is well-defined and is indeed the inverse of $\phi$.
:::

### Differentials for field extensions
:::{#lem-differential-for-algebraic-separable-field-extensions name=""}
Let $L/K$ be a separable field extension. Then $\Omega_{L/K}=0$.
:::
:::{.proof}
For any $\alpha\in L$, there exists a polynomial $f\in K[x]$ such that $f(\alpha)=0$ and $f'(\alpha)\neq 0$. Then $f'(\alpha)d\alpha=df(\alpha)=0$, which implies $d\alpha=0$. Since $\Omega_{L/K}$ is generated by $d\alpha$ for $\alpha\in L$, we have $\Omega_{L/K}=0$.
:::

:::{#lem-differential-for-purely-inseparable-field-extensions name=""}
Let $L/K$ be a purely inseparable field extension. Then $\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0$.
:::
:::{.proof}
Assume $\text{char}(K)=p>0$. By the transitivity sequence and the structure of purely inseparable extensions, we may assume $L=K[x]/(x^p-a)$ for some $a\in K$. By @lem-derivation-of-polynomial-ring, we have $\Omega_{L/K}\cong L\,dx/(px^{p-1}\,dx)=L\,dx\neq 0$.
:::

:::{#lem-differential-for-separable-trancendantal-extensions name=""}
If $L/K$ is separably genrated by $t_1,\cdots,t_n\in K$, then $\Omega_{L/K}$ is a free $L$-module generated by $dt_1,\cdots, dt_n$.
:::
:::{.proof}
By @lem-derivation-of-polynomial-ring and localization, we have 
$$\Omega_{K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)/K}\cong K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\,dt_1\oplus\cdots\oplus K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\,dt_n.$$ 

By @lem-differential-for-algebraic-separable-field-extensions, we have $\Omega_{L/K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)}=0$, which implies $\Omega_{L/K}\cong L\,dt_1+\cdots+ L\,dt_n$ by the transitivity sequence. It remains to show that $dt_1,\cdots, dt_n$ are linearly independent over $L$. We will prove this by showing that there exist $K$ derivations $d_i$ such that $d_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}$. For any $i$, we can extend the derivation $\frac{\partial}{\partial t_i}$ on $K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)$ to a derivation $d_i$ on $L$ by using the fact that $L/K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)$ is separable. To be precise, if $\alpha\in L$ is algebraic over $K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)$, then there exists a polynomial $f\in K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)[x]$ such that $f(\alpha)=0$ and $f'(\alpha)\neq 0$. We can define $d_i(\alpha)$ to be the unique solution of the equation $f'(\alpha)d_i(\alpha)+d_i(f)(\alpha)=0$. One can check that $d_i$ is indeed a derivation on $L$ and $d_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}$.
:::

### Relation to the cotangent space
:::{#lem-cotangent-space-is-fibre-of-differentials name=""}
Let $X$ be a scheme over $k$ and $x\in X$ be a closed point with residue field $\kappa (x)$ separable over $k$. Then the cotangent space of $X$ at $x$ is isomorphic to $\Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)$. 
:::
:::{.proof}
Apply the conormal sequence to the closed immersion $\operatorname{Spec}(k(x))\hookrightarrow X$, we have a map $\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2 \rightarrow \Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)$, where $\mathfrak m_x$ is the maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_{X,x}$. We will show this surjection is actually a bijection. For convenience, let $A=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ ,$k'=\kappa(x)$ and $\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_x$. Since the module of differentials is compatible with localization, it suffices to show that the map $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2 \rightarrow \Omega_{A/k}\otimes k'$ is a bijection. By Yoneda lemma, it suffices to show that for any $k'$-module $M$, the map 
$$
\operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(\Omega_{A/k}\otimes k', M)\to \operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2, M)
$$

is a bijection. By the universal property of $\Omega_{A/k}$, we have a bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_{A}(\Omega_{A/k}, M)\cong \operatorname{Der}_k(A,M)$. By @lem-differential-for-algebraic-separable-field-extensions, we have $\operatorname{Der}_k(k',M)=0$, which means that 
$$\operatorname{Der}_k(A,M)=\operatorname{Der}_{k'}(A,M)\cong \operatorname{Der}_{k'}(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2,M).$$

One checks that this is just the map defined above, and the last isomorphism will be shown when we discuss formally \etale.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="Variety case"}
In variety case, by @lem-derivation-of-polynomial-ring, we could deduce that $\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2$ and $\Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)$ both come from the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix. So they are isomorphic. 
:::

## Unramified morphisms
:::{#def-unramified-morphism name="unramified morphism"}
A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ between schemes is **unramified** if it is locally of finite type and $\Omega_{X/Y}=0$.
:::

By the transitivity sequence, unramified morphisms are stable under composition. By the base change property, unramified morphisms are stable under base change. One checks that unramified morphisms are also local on the target, so they are ``reasonable'' in the sense of the textbook the rising sea.

### Examples
By the above calculation of $\Omega_{A/B}$, we have the following corollaries.

:::{#cor-unramified-field-extensions name=""}
If $L/K$ is a field extension of finite type, then $\operatorname{Spec}(L) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(K)$ is unramified if and only if $L/K$ is a separable algebraic extension.
:::
:::{.proof}
By @lem-differential-for-algebraic-separable-field-extensions, it suffices to show that if $\operatorname{Spec}(L) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(K)$ is unramified then $L/K$ is a separable algebraic extension.

If $L/K$ is inseparable, then $\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0$ by the transitive exact sequence and @lem-differential-for-purely-inseparable-field-extensions. Thus, $L/K$ is separable. If $L/K$ is trancendental, then $\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0$ by @lem-differential-for-separable-trancendantal-extensions. Therefore, the extension $L/K$ must be algebraic separable.
:::
